extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / early-18th-century literate coffeehouse public
extracted.subtask_description: Early-18th-century periodical essays and literary criticism discussing standards for description, characterization, poetic diction, dedications/patronage, and reporting. The text mixes satire and prescriptive remarks about good taste and method in writing and reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lively battle narrative phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of abrupt, repeated phrases and colloquialisms ('Ditto,' 'And so,' 'But soon,' 'But having,' 'But could not,' 'But are,' 'But they,' 'Finds the party to have found') gives great life and spirit to the relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author praises a report of an 'Exercise at Arms' for its style and invention, noting that such elegant expressions 'do certainly give great life and spirit to the relation.' Example: the quoted marching, halting, wheeling and skirmishing description—though partly comic—demonstrates how terse connective phrases animate a military account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Battle accounts should instruct as well as describe
rubrics_metrics.description: A good account of a battle (or exercise) may 'instruct generals and their historians, both in fighting a battle, and describing it when it is over.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The satirical exercise is held up as a model for both the conduct of operations (subdividing, choosing ground) and for the manner of recounting them; descriptive invention can serve pedagogic ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive jangling wit that obscures meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Writings wrapped up in 'so much jingle and pun' (the wit of former times) can make a piece 'scarce intelligible', though the design may be sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the commentator's great-grandfather's treatise on bribery contains fine things but is made hard to understand by period wordplay; clarity of design should not be sacrificed to verbal trickery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy as mirror of an age's taste
rubrics_metrics.description: There is 'no method in the world of knowing the taste of an age... so good, as by the observations of the persons represented in their comedies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic characters should reflect contemporary manners; critics and historians can gauge a period's sensibilities by how people are depicted on stage (e.g., Ben Jonson's fop who smokes as a mark of foppery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage women should reflect social reality of their time
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakespeare's comparatively small role for women in dialogue is not poverty of genius but accurate reflection: 'he drew women as they then were in life... mothers, sisters, daughters, and wives.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwrights should portray female characters in accordance with the freedoms and roles available to women in the period depicted; modern drama may rightly present new female types (wits, politicians, coquettes) as social conditions change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization: virtue without affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: An ideal feminine character (Aspasia) 'is the most exact economist, without appearing busy; the most strictly virtuous, without tasting the praise of it; and shuns applause with as much industry, as others do reproach.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good character portrayals show qualities (economy, virtue, humility) naturally and without ostentation; such subtlety fixes a character in the reader's mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid characters whose virtue is merely performative
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters like Poluglossa—'acquainted with all the world but herself... innocence is only a restraint, with a certain mixture of envy'—are morally hollow and unworthy models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should distinguish genuine virtue from mere reputational innocence; dramatists should avoid creating characters whose virtue exists only as commentary on others' vices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid panegyrical dedications and insincere flattery
rubrics_metrics.description: Dedications commonly become panegyrical performance and risk being mistaken for flattery: 'the plain justice I have done you should, by my proceeding and others' mistaken judgment, be imagined flattery, a thing the bluntness of my nature does not care to be concerned with.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and critics are warned of the 'general vice' of over-praising patrons; dedications often function as commerce (satirically noted) rather than honest critical judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make scientific and philosophical exposition lively
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy and science have laboured under imputation of dryness; there is merit in writing 'a system of philosophy in a more lively method, both as to the matter and language.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites a planned fable-like explanatory method (dancing atoms, deities, a playful hypothesis of gravity) as an example of making abstruse subjects engaging without losing substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: The true sublime favors natural, fitting similes
rubrics_metrics.description: Forced similes in tragedy are 'forced and constrained'; it is 'proper and natural' for a poet to relieve thought with simile, but such comparisons should not honor the brute rather than the hero (ancient similes like rock or Lybian lion may be 'stupid and inanimate').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique favors novel, contextually appropriate similes (example given: the 'ministering angel' simile in 'The Campaign' that suits both sedate and active courage), and warns against tired classical figures that fail modern readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: A poem may and should function as chronicle
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful heroic poem can be 'a chronicle as well as a poem,' preserving the memory of a hero when monuments fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ideal national/occasional poem combines familiar narrative clarity with elevated heroic diction so it serves both record and art (illustrated by praise of 'The Campaign').

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirize and avoid formulaic, space-filling reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Periodical writers are forced into 'hard shifts' that fill papers with repetitive orders of battle; a westerly wind can cause every paper to range its men 'in squadrons and battalions'—a comment on routine reportage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should be cautious of repeating formulaic military copy to fill space; originality of account and attention to what matters (names, consequences) are implied virtues.
